name: David K - May 2
transcript:
Therapist: David, good to see you. How are things with the medication adjustment?

David: The new dosage seems to be working better. The brain fog from the first two weeks has cleared up. I actually feel more like myself now.

Therapist: That's encouraging. When you say more like yourself, what does that mean specifically?

David: I have energy again. Like, I actually wanted to cook dinner last night instead of just ordering takeout. And I went for a run on Saturday. First time in months.

Therapist: Those are really concrete markers of improvement. The motivation to engage with daily activities is often one of the first things depression takes and one of the last things to come back. How about your mood overall?

David: It's more stable. I'm not having those crashes in the evening anymore where everything just feels hopeless. I still have low moments but they pass. They don't swallow the whole day.

Therapist: That's an important distinction. The goal of the medication isn't to eliminate all sadness but to restore your emotional range and resilience. It sounds like that's happening.

David: Yeah. I think so. My wife noticed too. She said I seem more present, like I'm actually in the room instead of somewhere else.

Therapist: How are things between you two? Last time you mentioned some tension.

David: Better. We actually had a real conversation last weekend about what the last six months have been like. I apologized for being so withdrawn and she said she was just relieved I was getting help. She wasn't angry, just scared.

Therapist: That vulnerability from both sides is really valuable. Depression often creates distance in relationships because the person withdrawing doesn't have the energy for connection, and the partner can't tell if it's about them.

David: Exactly. She thought I was unhappy with her or the marriage. I had no idea she was carrying that.

Therapist: Now that things are stabilizing, do you want to talk about what you think triggered this episode? You mentioned it started around October.

David: I think it was the job change. I left a role where I was really confident and respected, and went to this new company where I felt like I was starting from zero. And then my dad had that health scare around the same time. It was like the ground shifted under me.

Therapist: Multiple stressors simultaneously, especially ones that challenge your sense of competence and safety, can overwhelm your coping capacity. Have you settled in at the new job now?

David: Yeah, actually. I got good feedback on my last project and I feel like people know who I am now. The imposter syndrome has mostly faded. I think the depression was making me interpret everything negatively, so normal new-job adjustment felt like failure.

Therapist: That's great insight. Depression acts like a filter that amplifies negative signals and mutes positive ones. As the depression lifts, you can see the same situation more accurately.

David: I want to make sure this doesn't happen again. Like, what are the warning signs I should watch for?

Therapist: Great question. Let's build your early warning system. Based on this episode, what were the first changes you noticed?

David: I stopped exercising first. Then I started canceling plans with friends. Then the sleep got bad, staying up too late scrolling my phone. By the time I realized something was wrong I was already deep in it.

Therapist: So withdrawal from physical activity and social connection, followed by sleep disruption. Those are your personal red flags. If you notice two of those three happening for more than a week, that's your cue to take action, whether that's calling me, talking to your wife, or even just naming it to yourself.

David: That's really helpful to have spelled out. I think I knew something was wrong for months but I kept telling myself I was just tired or busy.

Therapist: Denial is another common companion of depression. Having a concrete checklist makes it harder to rationalize away. And David, your wife can be an ally here too. Would you be comfortable giving her those three red flags so she can gently flag it if she notices?

David: Yeah, that's a good idea. I'll talk to her about it tonight.

Therapist: Excellent. Let's meet again in three weeks to check on the medication and continue this work. You're making great progress.

David: Thanks. I actually look forward to these sessions now instead of dreading them. That's probably a good sign.

Therapist: It definitely is. See you in three weeks.
